prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands in twisted bilayer graphene at a magic angle and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: one prize part, B025, credited to Jarillo-Herrero, MacDonald and Bistritzer. After the full first round I can state the discovery more narrowly than before, and the narrower statement is the one I would defend. The credited discovery is that a single continuously tunable geometric parameter, the twist angle, brings a bilayer to a regime where flat bands exist and where correlated insulating states and gate-tunable superconductivity appear at the predicted angle. That is a prediction (the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model) followed by an unambiguous experiment (2018) on a system that theory and experiment could both control. The phenomena are reproduced by many groups and carried over to several moire platforms. Whether the pairing mechanism is phonon-mediated, electronic or something else is a separate question, which I would not ask the citation to settle. The chair asks whether the open mechanism counts against B025 only as timing. My answer is that it bears on how far the citation can reach, not on whether the observed phases are secure. Several earlier prizes honoured an observed phase whose microscopic origin was open. The wording below names only the flat-band prediction and the observed phases, so it does not imply any mechanism and does not imply that flat-band signatures were never seen before 2018.
statement.case_against: Three objections stay serious. First, maturity: eight years is short, and twist-angle disorder makes sample-to-sample reproducibility uneven. I have weighed this against the replication evidence and still think the established core is secure, but it is a judgment and Danielsson, Kroll, Lindroth and Olsson are entitled to weigh it differently. Second, attribution: the three-name cap leaves out Andrei, whose early scanning-probe evidence of flat bands and van Hove singularities in small-angle twisted bilayers is a real experimental contribution, and Bistritzer's seat is the most contestable one in my configuration. I keep him because the magic angle is a result of the continuum model he co-authored, and dropping him would credit a joint prediction to one theorist. I would accept Andrei in that seat if the committee decided to credit early experimental flat-band evidence over the second theorist. Third, the more mature B013 has a longer confirmation record, so if the committee judges the moire field too young it is the right fallback, with the citation limited to the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect.

responses.point: Danielsson now prefers B013 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, and argues that topological insulators have almost twice the confirmation time and a stable interpretation, while B025 depends on an unresolved mechanism and on Andrei's competing claim.
responses.response: I accept that B013 has a longer record and that Danielsson's move from B033 to the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio is the right correction, because the Z2 paper is the conceptual core. We differ on what maturity requires. If the credited discovery is the observed phases rather than the pairing mechanism, then the question is whether those phases are reproducible, and they have been, across independent groups and several platforms. Confirmation time is a proxy for that and not the criterion itself. On Andrei, I agree that no three-name set resolves the claim. B013 has the same problem with Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and Hasan, so I do not think attribution separates the two ballots in Danielsson's favour. I do not claim B025 is cleaner on every point, only that the prediction-and-discovery mapping onto three names is the more direct one.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B013 first as a prediction-then-confirmation chain, confirmed for nearly two decades, and notes that five of the opening ballots proposed the same Kane-Mele-Molenkamp trio, so it is the least contested on names.
responses.response: The agreement on the trio is real, and I do not dismiss it. Agreement on three names does not settle whether three names describe the discovery. Olsson's own statement says that Hasan's three-dimensional identification is arguably an equally decisive experiment and that Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang are outside the set, so the compound structure is on the page in her own words. For B025, the Andrei question concerns who else should share an otherwise coherent prediction-and-discovery pair. For B013 the question is whether the discovery is split between 2D and 3D, which is more fundamental. I would support B013 with a citation limited to the 2D quantum spin Hall effect if the committee found B025 premature. Olsson argues that overlap with the 2016 prize is limited, and I agree. I do not put B013 behind B025 for that reason.

responses.point: Kroll says attribution cleanliness should outrank the number of members who ranked a candidate, and argues that the lattice clock has a cleaner two-name credit than the topological-insulator or graphene ballots.
responses.response: I agree with the principle and have tried to apply it to my own ballot. A count of supporters should not stand in for a scientific case, and I do not treat the opening ballots as evidence of merit. The Katori-Ye pairing is clean, and the split between concept and demonstration is natural. My difficulty is the other half of the choice. A lattice clock sharpens a measurement of a frequency that has been measured with increasing precision since the prizes of 2005 and 2012, so the new knowledge lies in the accuracy reached. B025 reports phases of matter that were not known to exist in such a system. A prize can go to either kind of advance, but when the attribution problems are comparable, I give the discovery of a new regime the greater weight. I also think B025's attribution is contested, not unclean: three names cover one prediction and one experiment, and the edge is Andrei's claim.

responses.point: Johansson, who now supports the Bistritzer trio, warns that a cleaner configuration is not necessarily a more accurate account of history and asks that the citation name both the prediction and the discovery without implying a single origin.
responses.response: That caution is right and I have followed it. The citation joins two clauses, the prediction of flat bands at a magic angle and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states, and each clause is assigned to the people who did that part. It makes no claim about who first saw flat-band signatures or van Hove singularities, so it stays true if Andrei's contribution is later given more weight. I agree with Johansson that Andrei's claim is open. I would rather say this openly in the discussion than let the three-name cap look like a finding that her work did not matter. I also agree that B013 is the messier attribution of my two candidates, for the reasons Johansson gives.

responses.point: The chair, who has moved B025 to the head of his configuration, observes that B025 is the candidate that depends most on judging that the established core is robust enough, and asks whether a field-neutral rule should govern how recent nearby prizes bear on novelty.
responses.response: The chair's remark that B025 depends most on that judgment is correct, and I would rather state it than hide it. My answer to the question on a rule is yes, and I would phrase it this way: a nearby earlier prize counts against novelty only if it honoured the same discovery or the same advance. On that test the 2016 topological-phases prize does not cover the quantum spin Hall effect in HgTe, the 2025 circuits prize does not cover moire materials, and the 2005 and 2012 prizes do not cover magic-wavelength lattice trapping, though they are closer to B006 than the others. The rule does not favour B025 over B013, and I would apply it to all the ballots. The superconducting mechanism affects what the citation says, not whether a prize can be given.

responses.point: Lindroth asks whether the support for B025 and topological insulators among five members reflects scientific weight or a shared condensed-matter vantage, and notes that attribution leaves out someone with a documented claim in either choice of third name.
responses.response: The first point deserves an answer, because I am not a condensed-matter physicist, which is relevant here. My own field is statistical physics of complex systems, and my interest in B025 is not that of a specialist in the material. What attracts me is that one control parameter puts a strongly interacting system in front of theory and experiment together. Members from atomic, quantum-technology and high-energy backgrounds also ranked it, so I do not think the support is purely a matter of vantage, but I cannot exclude some effect. I agree that no third seat avoids leaving out someone with a claim, and I think it is better to say so than to claim the choice is clean. I take the point about the redefinition of the second: I would not hold B006 against its undecided status, but it does not change my view that B025 is the stronger discovery.

uncertainties: Whether Andrei should hold the third seat in place of Bistritzer. My account of the twisted-bilayer attribution history rests on general knowledge and the supplied statements, not on primary sources, and I have not changed this view since round 1.
Whether the committee accepts that the discovery is the set of observed phases and not the pairing mechanism, and so judges a citation limited to those phases to be safe.
Whether eight years is enough, given that the superconducting mechanism and twist-angle disorder are still open; B013 would be the fallback if the committee decides it is not.
Whether a field-neutral rule on recent nearby prizes will be adopted, and whether it would change the weight given to B006 or B013.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict has arisen since round 1. My work on turbulence, cloud microphysics, random matrices and neural networks is not in the shortlisted fields, and none of the credited names on B025, B013 or B002 is among my listed co-authors, supervisors or institutions. I note that I am not a condensed-matter specialist, so my judgment of the materials physics relies on colleagues who are. I did not change my preferred configuration in round 2: the first-round exchange sharpened the wording of the citation but did not change my assessment.
